passage:
Friday, 9 p.m. Three people, three different conversations today. Lakshmi has run client accounts for nine years, so I told her the goal and left the route to her. She said, “Good. I'll send you a summary on Friday.” Rohan joined two weeks ago and looked lost, so I sat with him for an hour and went through his first client call step by step. Then Sneha's report had two real mistakes. I told her straight and kindly, the same way I'd tell Lakshmi.

Before leaving I asked each of them, “What would help you most from me next week?” Lakshmi wanted fewer meetings. Rohan wanted a checklist. Sneha wanted feedback earlier. What suits me is a weekly meeting for everyone. It wouldn't have worked.
— Jagdish

qa.q: How long has Lakshmi run client accounts?
qa.a: Lakshmi has run client accounts for nine years.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish give Lakshmi the goal and leave the route to Lakshmi?
qa.a: Lakshmi is experienced and works well with freedom, so Jagdish trusted Lakshmi with the route.

qa.q: What choice did Jagdish make before leaving that helped fit each person?
qa.a: Jagdish asked each person what would help most from Jagdish next week.

qa.q: What might Rohan have felt when Jagdish sat down for an hour and went through the first client call?
qa.a: Rohan probably felt relieved and supported, since Rohan looked lost and needed guidance.

grounding: A leader gives freedom to the experienced, guidance to the new and honest feedback to all, asking each person what they need.

passage:
Omkar: Bidisha, quick check. First month done. What do you need from me?
Bidisha: honestly a bit more structure? I don't always know what “done” looks like
Omkar: got it. I'll write down done-criteria for your tasks tomorrow and we'll go through them together on Thursday
Bidisha: thank you 🙂
Omkar: Tanmay, you've done this for years so I'll stay out of your way. Is that still right?
Tanmay: yes please, just shout if the client changes scope
Omkar: deal. And one thing for both of you: if my feedback ever feels off, say so
Bidisha: will do
Tanmay: 👍

qa.q: What did Bidisha ask for more of?
qa.a: Bidisha asked for a bit more structure.

qa.q: What does Bidisha mean by saying, “I don't always know what ‘done’ looks like”?
qa.a: Bidisha feels unsure of expectations as a newcomer and wants clear criteria to feel confident.

qa.q: What did Omkar promise Bidisha?
qa.a: Omkar promised to write done-criteria for Bidisha's tasks the next day and go through them together on Thursday.

qa.q: How might Tanmay see Omkar's decision to stay out of the way?
qa.a: Tanmay probably feels trusted and respected as an experienced member, and glad not to be micromanaged.

grounding: A leader asks each team member what they need and gives structure to the new and freedom to the experienced.

passage:
At the farm extension office in a village near Dharwad, Santosh had just become the team head. His three field staff were very different.
Nikita had worked there eight years and knew every farmer by name. He told her, “You plan your own visits this month. Just tell me where you'll be.” She smiled.
Raju had joined two weeks ago. Santosh went with him to the first three farms, showed him how to test soil, and checked his forms every evening.
Farzana was good but always late with reports. Santosh told her plainly, kindly, “Your advice to farmers is excellent. Your reports are a week late. What would help?”
By the end of the month, each had asked for something different, and each had got it.

qa.q: How long had Nikita worked at the office?
qa.a: Eight years.

qa.q: How might Raju have felt with Santosh going to the farms with him?
qa.a: He probably felt supported and less nervous in his first weeks, learning by doing alongside his boss.

qa.q: Why does Santosh's approach work for all three staff?
qa.a: He gives freedom to the experienced, guidance to the new and honest feedback to everyone, based on what each needs.

qa.q: How might Farzana feel after Santosh's feedback?
qa.a: She might feel respected rather than scolded, since he praised her strength and asked what would help.

grounding: Shows a young leader giving freedom to an experienced staff member, guidance to a new one and honest feedback to all.

passage:
Abebe had become shift lead at the coffee roastery in Addis Ababa in March. He noticed quickly that one style didn't fit everyone.
Layla had roasted beans for ten years. When he tried to show her a new timer, she frowned. So he stepped back. “You know this better than me. Tell me if you need anything.”
Samuel, the new boy, was nervous around the big roaster. Abebe stood beside him for a whole week, explaining each step.
With both of them, he was honest. He told Layla her batch logs were missing details, and told Samuel he was too slow on packing.
At the end of the month, Layla said, “You're the first lead who didn't try to teach me my own job.” Samuel said, “You're the first who actually taught me.”

qa.q: How long had Layla roasted beans?
qa.a: For ten years.

qa.q: How did Layla seem to feel when Abebe tried to show her a new timer?
qa.a: She seemed irritated and a bit insulted, frowning at being taught what she already knew.

qa.q: What did Abebe do that fit each person's needs?
qa.a: He gave Layla freedom, guided Samuel closely and gave both honest feedback, adjusting his style to each.

qa.q: How might Samuel have felt during his first week?
qa.a: He was probably nervous at first but reassured, since Abebe stood beside him and explained each step.

grounding: Shows a young shift lead giving freedom to an expert, guidance to a newcomer and honest feedback to both.

passage:
Tenzin had just been made team leader over four receptionists at the hotel's front desk.
Mrs D'Souza had worked the desk for twenty years. Tenzin asked her, “How do you want to handle the tour groups?” and let her run them her way.
Akash had joined last month from a village near Shimla. He was scared of angry guests. Tenzin sat beside him on the evening shift and whispered what to say.
Neeta was fast and friendly but kept forgetting to update the booking system. Tenzin told her directly: “Your guests love you. The system needs updating every time, though. Let's set a reminder.”
In the staff room, Akash said, “Tenzin sir asks each of us what we need. The last boss only told us what he wanted.”

qa.q: Where had Akash joined from?
qa.a: From a village near Shimla.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt with Tenzin sitting beside him?
qa.a: He probably felt supported and less scared of angry guests.

qa.q: Why is asking "what do you need" a strong leadership habit?
qa.a: It lets Tenzin give freedom, guidance or feedback to each person as they need, instead of treating everyone the same.

qa.q: How might Mrs D'Souza feel about being asked how she wants to handle the tour groups?
qa.a: She would likely feel respected and trusted after twenty years on the desk.

grounding: Shows a young team leader giving freedom to the experienced, guidance to the new and honest feedback to all, based on need.

passage:
Tenzin,
Congratulations on the new team! You asked how I manage mine without going mad.
Honestly, I used to run everyone the same way: daily check-ins, detailed notes on everything. Leela, who's been here eight years, told me politely it felt like being watched. Kabir, who'd just joined, told me nothing at all, and was quietly drowning.
So I started asking each person one question: "What do you need from me this month?" Leela said: leave me alone, review at the end. Now she gets a Friday chat and full freedom. Kabir said he didn't know where to start, so we sit together fifteen minutes each morning and I show him how I'd break a task down. Everyone, Leela included, still gets honest feedback when something isn't working, just in different doses.
It's more work at first. It's much less work later.
Call me after your first week.
Abhinav

qa.q: How long has Leela been there?
qa.a: Eight years.

qa.q: What was Kabir feeling in the early weeks?
qa.a: Kabir felt lost and overwhelmed, "quietly drowning", but didn't say anything.

qa.q: What question did Abhinav start asking, and why does it work?
qa.a: "What do you need from me this month?"; it lets each person get the right mix of freedom and guidance instead of one habit for all.

qa.q: How did Leela experience Abhinav's old style?
qa.a: Leela felt watched and a little stifled, as if eight years of experience counted for nothing.

grounding: Shows a leader who asks each person what they need, giving freedom to the experienced, guidance to the new and honest feedback to everyone.
